title: Efficient cause: Trinity immediately; Christ specially; angels as ministers

The raising belonging toward ye dead stands as a merely divine work, far surpassing every power belonging toward creatures (Dionysius On ye Divine Names ch.
pass_b_english: The raising of the dead is a merely divine work, far surpassing every power of creatures (Dionysius On the Divine Names ch. 6), and therefore proceeds immediately from God, as prefigured in Ezek. 37:12. The Father raises (Rom. 8:11; 1 Cor. 6:14; 2 Cor. 4:14); the Son (John 5:28; ch. 6; 11:25); the Holy Spirit with the same power (Rom. 8:11). Although the Holy Trinity is commonly the cause of the resurrection, yet Christ is specially so (John 6:54) — both as exemplar cause and because his most powerful voice is instrumental cause. If resurrection is taken strictly, it is God's immediate work; if more loosely for the whole complex before and after, angels may be called ministers and instruments (Matt. 24:31). We reject Richard and Scotus who thought nature could be a cause of the resurrection.
source_text: Resuscitatio mortuorum est opus mere divinum, longissime exsuperans omnem creaturarum virtutem, ut docet Dionysius cap. 6. de div. nominibus, ideoque immediate a Deo proficiscitur, ut praefiguratum est Ezech. 37.v.12. Pater presentat Rom. 8.v.11; 1 Cor. 6.v.14; 2 Cor. 4.v.14. Filius Joh. 5.v.28 & c.6 & 11.v.25. Spiritus Sanctus eadem vi Rom. 8.v.11. Etsi S. Trinitas communiter resurrectionis causa sit, tamen Christus est singulariter, Joh. 6.54. tum quia est causa exemplaris, tum quia potentissima vox ejus est causa instrumentalis. Si resurrectio stricte sumatur, est opus Dei immediatum; si laxius pro toto complexu ante & post, angeli resurrectionis ministri & instrumenta dici possunt, Matth. 24.v.31. Rejicimus errorem Richardi & Scoti qui putaverunt naturam resurrectionis causam esse posse.
